newsitem.title: GERMANY: German post office, postal bank end dispute.
newsitem.headline: German post office, postal bank end dispute.

text.p: The post and banking arms of the former Deutsche Bundespost ended an angry feud on Wednesday, signing a cooperation deal that continues their symbiotic relationship and paves the way for a bourse listing.

Deutsche Post AG and Deutsche Postbank AG, tightly-wed agencies that emerged from the restructuring of the Bundespost as two separate companies, have fought bitterly for the past two years over post office efforts to take control of its sister agency.

Post and Telecommunications Minister Wolfgang Boetsch welcomed the signing, which came after a breakthrough in government coalition talks on the issue in February, saying the deal created a sound basis for future cooperation.
"Beyond that the agreement ensures the privatisation of both companies, whereby the federal government is determined to list Postbank on the bourse as soon as possible," he said.
Deutsche Bundespost, the former post and telecommunications agency, was broken up in 1989 into three agencies with a combined workforce that was larger than the German army.

In 1995 these three agencies became joint stock companies fully-owned by the government. Deutsche Telekom, the telecoms arm, listed over a quarter of its capital on stock exchanges last November in Europe's largest-ever initial public offering.
The privatisation of the Postbank and later the Post Office were supposed to follow by 1998, but the government soon found that divorcing the two partners was extremely difficult.

The Deutsche Reichspost first began offering banking services under the Nazi government in 1939, following the model of other European countries, and creating a cheap, flexible savings and checking system.

But even though the importance of the postal banking services grew in the post-war period, the postal bank remained tied to the post office. It shared staff with the post office and offered its services over post office counters.
This created a symbiotic relationship between the two.
While Post AG could not afford to run its sprawling network of post offices without revenue from Postbank, the bank has no independent branch offices of its own.
In the battle that ensued, Postbank sought to prevent the Post Office from gaining excessive influence over its banking business and to keep fees for using Post Office counter space to a minimum.
In the end a political compromise was reached that would allow Post AG to take a stake of up to 17.5 percent in Postbank in 1998 that would not allow it to exercise control.
Postbank agreed under pressure to pay its landlord 1.1 billion marks ($638.1 million) this year for use of post office facilities.

Under pressure to put a cap on yawning budget deficits ahead of European monetary union, Finance Minister Theo Waigel would like to privatise the Postbank this year, hoping to rake in billions from the sale. Post AG would follow in 1999. This fee is set to fall to 750 million marks over four years.
Klaus Zumwinkel, Post AG chairman, said the compromise was acceptable to all sides.
"It is important for our employees that we have a clear basis and can go forward together with the management of the Postbank," he told Germany's N-TV all-news channel.
German press reports said Postbank chairman Guenter Schneider, who was not present at the signing, was planning to step down in protest. The Postbank called these reports "pure speculation".
"We consider the proposal a fair compromise: that is why we signed," said Achim Scholz, a Postbank board member.
-- Bonn Newsroom, 49 228 26097 150 ($ = 1.723 German Marks)
